title: Master of All Masters
text:
This was back in the days when Our Lord and Saint Peter still went walking about on the earth. One day they came to a forge.

The blacksmith there had made a bargain with the Devil. For seven years he was to be master of all masters in the smith’s craft, and when the seven years were up, the Devil would have him. It was all set down in a contract, and both of them had signed it. That was why the blacksmith had painted over his door, in letters you could read from the road: “Here lives the Master of All Masters!”

Our Lord read it and went in.

“Who are you?” he asked.

“Read what it says over the door,” said the blacksmith. “Though I don’t suppose you can read. In that case you’ll just have to wait till somebody comes along who can help you.”

Before Our Lord could answer, a man came along leading a horse he wanted shod.

“Might I be allowed to shoe it?” asked Our Lord.

“You can try,” said the blacksmith. “You can’t make such a botch of it that I can’t put it right again.”

So Our Lord went out to the horse and took off one of its forelegs, as easily as you’d pull off a mitten. He laid the leg deep among the coals, where it came to no harm, and heated the shoe until it glowed. Then he set the leg on the anvil and fitted the red-hot shoe, drove the nails home and clinched them, while sparks flew and coal smoke curled up to the rafters. After that he put the leg back on the horse, as whole and sound as ever. The horse stood on three legs and waited. When the first foreleg was done, he took off the other and did the very same. Then came the hind legs, first the right and then the left: into the fire, shoe glowing, nails clinched, and back on again.

The blacksmith stood by the open door and watched. For once in his life he had nothing to say.

“You’re not a bad smith, you know,” he said at last.

“Do you think so?” said Our Lord.

A little later the blacksmith’s mother came over to the forge to tell him his dinner was on the table. She was very old, bent nearly double, with a face as wrinkled as a winter apple, and she could barely put one foot in front of the other.

“Now mark what you see,” said Our Lord.

He took hold of the old woman, laid her in the forge, and out of her he forged a lovely young girl.

“I’ll say what I said before,” said the blacksmith. “You’re no bad smith at all. It says over my door that here lives the Master of All Masters, but I’ll tell you straight: live and learn.” And off he went to eat his dinner.

When he got back to the forge, a man came riding up who wanted his horse shod.

“That’ll soon be done,” said the blacksmith. “I’ve just learned a new way of shoeing. It comes in very handy when the days are short.”

And he set about cutting and wrenching until he had all four legs off the horse at once. “I can’t see the sense in fiddling about with one at a time,” he said. He laid the legs in the fire, just as he had seen Our Lord do, heaped on plenty of coal, and set his apprentices working the bellows for all they were worth.

But it went the way you might expect. The legs burned to cinders, and the blacksmith had to pay for the horse.

He didn’t much care for that. But just then a poor old beggar woman came walking by, and he thought: if the one thing won’t work, the other surely will. He took hold of the old woman and laid her in the forge, and for all her crying and begging for her life, it did her no good.

“You don’t know what’s good for you, old as you are,” said the blacksmith. “In a moment you’ll be a young girl again, and I won’t charge you so much as a penny for the work.”

It went no better for the poor old woman than it had for the horse’s legs.
imagePrompt: Inside a sooty village forge, Our Lord—a calm wanderer—holds a horse’s severed foreleg steady on the anvil-block while a horseshoe glows red-hot beside it. Sparks and coal-smoke swirl as he fits the shoe with effortless precision, and the proud Blacksmith, broad-shouldered and grimy with soot, watches in stunned silence near the open forge door.

title: The Devil in the Pear Tree
text:
“That was ill done,” said Our Lord.

“Oh, there aren’t many who’ll ask after her,” said the blacksmith. “But the Devil ought to be ashamed of himself. He promised I’d be master of all masters, and he’s barely keeping his end of the bargain.”

“If you could have three wishes from me,” said Our Lord, “what would you wish for?”

“Try me and you’ll find out,” said the blacksmith.

So Our Lord granted him three wishes.

“Then first of all,” said the blacksmith, pointing out at the pear tree that grew by the forge wall, “I wish that whoever I ask to climb up that pear tree must stay sitting there until I myself ask him to come down again.” He jerked his thumb towards the workshop. “Second, I wish that whoever I ask to sit in my armchair in there must stay sitting in it until I myself ask him to get up again.” Last of all he patted his pocket. “And third, I wish that whoever I ask to crawl into this steel-wire purse of mine must stay inside until I myself give him leave to crawl out again.”

“You wished like a fool,” said Saint Peter. “First and foremost you should have wished for God’s grace and friendship.”

“I didn’t dare aim so high,” said the blacksmith.

Then Our Lord and Saint Peter said goodbye and went on their way.

Time went by, as time will, and when the seven years were up, the Devil came to fetch the blacksmith, just as the contract said. He poked his nose in at the forge door.

“Are you ready now?” he said.

“Oh, I really must put a head on this nail first,” said the blacksmith. “Why don’t you climb up the pear tree while you wait, and pick yourself a pear to chew on? You must be hungry and thirsty after your journey.”

The Devil thanked him kindly and climbed up. It was late in the summer, and the pears hung fat and golden in the evening sun. He settled himself on a branch and reached for the biggest pear of all, and there he stuck. He couldn’t climb up and he couldn’t climb down.

Below him stood the blacksmith, arms folded, with the anvil and his tools about his feet and a sly grin on his face.

“Well, now that I think it over properly,” he said, “I won’t get a head on this nail for the next four years. This iron is the very devil to work. You can’t come down before then, but you can sit up there and have a nice long rest.”

The Devil begged and pleaded, in a voice as thin as a worn penny, to be let down, but it did no good. In the end he had to promise not to come back until the four years were up, just as the blacksmith had said.

“Well, then you may come down,” said the blacksmith.
imagePrompt: By the forge wall, the Devil is stuck high in a leaf-heavy pear tree, bristling with frustration as he clings to a branch and cannot climb down. Below, the Blacksmith stands with arms folded and a sly, satisfied grin, the anvil and tools scattered nearby, late sunlight catching on pears and iron.

title: The Steel-Wire Purse
text:
When the four years were up, the Devil was back.

“Now you must be ready,” he said. “Surely you’ve put a head on that nail by now.”

“Oh, it’s got its head all right,” said the blacksmith, “but you’re a tiny bit early all the same, for I haven’t sharpened the point yet. I’ve never forged such hard iron in all my life. While I put a point on it, why don’t you sit in my armchair and rest? You must be tired, I should think.”

“Don’t mind if I do,” said the Devil, and he sat down in the armchair.

But he had hardly stretched out his legs before the blacksmith said that, now he came to think it over properly, he couldn’t possibly get the point sharpened for another four years.

At first the Devil asked nicely to be let out of the chair. Then he lost his temper and started making threats. But the blacksmith made his excuses as best he could. It was the iron’s fault, he said, for it was so fiendishly hard. And he comforted the Devil by telling him how snug and cosy he was in that armchair, and that in four years he would be free to go, to the very minute.

There was nothing else for it. The Devil had to promise not to come for the blacksmith until the four years were up.

“Well, then you may get up again,” said the blacksmith, and the Devil was off as fast as his legs would carry him.

Four years later the Devil came back once more and poked his nose in at the forge door.

“Now you’re ready, I know you are,” he said.

“Ready and waiting,” said the blacksmith. “We can go whenever you like. But listen,” he went on, “there’s something I’ve been meaning to ask you for a long time. Is it true, what people say, that the Devil can make himself as small as he likes?”

“Heaven knows it is,” said the Devil.

“Oh, then you could do me a favour,” said the blacksmith. He held out his steel-wire purse, wide open in his big, calloused hands. “Crawl into this and see if the bottom’s sound. I’m so afraid of losing my travelling money.”

“Gladly,” said the Devil. He made himself small and crawled in among the coins.

The moment he was inside, the blacksmith snapped the purse shut.

“Yes, it’s whole and tight all over,” said the Devil from inside the purse.

“Glad to hear it,” said the blacksmith. “But better safe than sorry. I think I’ll just weld the joints a bit, to make sure.” And he laid the purse in the forge and heated it till it glowed.

“Ow! Ow! Are you mad?” shrieked the Devil. “Don’t you know I’m in here?”

“I can’t help that,” said the blacksmith. “You know the old saying: strike while the iron is hot.” And he took his great sledgehammer, laid the purse on the anvil, and hammered away at it with all his might.

“Ow, ow, ow!” howled the Devil inside the purse. “For pity’s sake, just let me out, and I’ll never come back again!”

“Well, I suppose the joints are welded well enough now,” said the blacksmith. “You may come out.”

He opened the purse, and the Devil shot off so fast he didn’t even dare look back.
imagePrompt: In the dim workshop, the Devil—shrunken small—crawls into the Blacksmith’s steel-wire purse held open in the Blacksmith’s thick, calloused hands. The Blacksmith leans forward with bold, intent eyes, poised to snap it shut, while the forge behind them glows with a menacing orange heat.

title: Six Steps from Heaven
text:
But after a while it occurred to the blacksmith that it might not have been wise to make an enemy of the Devil. “For if I can’t get into the Kingdom of God,” he thought, “I could end up homeless, now that I’ve fallen out with the one who rules in Hell.” He decided he had better try to get in somewhere, Hell or Heaven, sooner rather than later, so that he would know where he stood. So he slung his sledgehammer over his shoulder and set off.

When he had walked a good long way, he came to the crossroads where the road to Heaven parts from the road to Hell. There he caught up with a journeyman tailor, who was scurrying along with his pressing iron in his hand.

“Good day,” said the blacksmith. “Where are you off to?”

“To Heaven, if they’ll let me in,” said the tailor. “And you?”

“Oh, then we won’t be keeping each other company for long,” said the blacksmith. “I thought I’d try Hell first. The Devil and I are a little acquainted.”

So they said goodbye and each went his own way. But the blacksmith was a big, strong man and walked a good deal faster than the tailor, and it wasn’t long before he stood at the gate of Hell. He told the guard to go in and say there was someone outside who would like a word with the Devil.

“Go out and ask who it is,” the Devil told the guard.

“Give the Devil my regards and tell him it’s the blacksmith with the purse. He’ll know,” said the blacksmith. “And ask him nicely to let me in at once, because I’ve been at my forge all morning, and I’ve walked a long way since.”

When the Devil got that message, he ordered the guard to lock all nine locks on the gate of Hell. “And put a padlock on as well,” he said, “for if he gets in, he’ll turn the whole of Hell upside down.”

Outside, the blacksmith heard the bolts shoot home, one after another.

“No refuge here, then,” he said to himself. “I’d better try Heaven.”

He turned round and tramped all the way back to the crossroads, and there he took the road the tailor had taken. He was cross about all that walking back and forth for nothing, so he lengthened his stride and went at it as hard as he could. He reached the gate of Heaven as Saint Peter was opening it a crack, just wide enough for the thin tailor to slip through sideways. Light spilled out through the gap. The blacksmith was still six or seven steps away.

“I’d better look sharp,” he thought. He grabbed his sledgehammer and hurled it through the gap in the gate at the very moment the tailor slipped in.

And if he didn’t get in through that opening, I’m sure I don’t know what became of him.
imagePrompt: At Heaven’s gate, Saint Peter cracks the door open just enough for the Journeyman Tailor—thin and travel-worn, clutching his pressing iron—to slip through sideways. Six steps away, the Blacksmith charges forward, muscles tense, hurling his heavy sledgehammer into the narrow opening as the bright threshold flares around the closing gap.
